ELEPHANT MOVEMENT & MIGRATION  |  RESEARCH REVIEW
Search cutoff: 25 October 2026
2
Scope and how to use this review
Selection approach
Priority was given to elephant movement, migration, ranging, dispersal and connectivity studies matching Sri
Lanka, satellite remote sensing or image processing, preferably published during 2020-2026. Close
supporting work on habitat change, HEC and detection was included because the direct intersection is
narrow. The 50 entries are distinct publications; conference, commentary and review evidence is identified
where relevant.
Search and verification
Public scholarly web searches, publisher pages, institutional repositories and citation chaining were used,
with Crossref records checked for author, title, venue and DOI metadata. Search families included elephant
migration Sri Lanka Sentinel, elephant movement satellite remote sensing, elephant corridor habitat
connectivity, and elephant detection satellite drone deep learning. The supplied PDF was read directly. A
Consensus lookup was attempted but its account search quota was exhausted; no records were obtained
from it.
Date policy
The search window ends on 25 October 2026. Journal issue years are used in the bibliography where
available. The national Sri Lanka survey [12] was online in 2019 and issued in 2021; the Thai seasonal study
[28] was online in December 2019 for the 2020 issue. These are clearly flagged boundary cases. Publication
in 2025 or 2026 does not imply that observations were collected then.
Evidence basis and interpretation
Each entry states the material actually assessed: the supplied full PDF, selected full-text sections, an
English abstract, or an abstract/publisher record. Access to a full paper was not possible for every entry. The
research-and-findings paragraph summarizes reported evidence. Gaps and future directions are reviewer
synthesis unless explicitly attributed to the authors. Limitations include both stated constraints and
reviewer cautions; missing detail in an abstract is not proof that the full study omitted it.
Reading order and tags
Read the Sri Lankan section first, then the Asian and African movement methods. The imaging and review
sections supply technical foundations. SL = Sri Lanka; SAT = Earth-observation satellite imagery or
satellite-derived layers; IP = image processing or image analysis (manual photo work is labeled); GPS =
animal telemetry; UAV = drone; SDM = species-distribution model; SIM = simulation. Satellite telemetry is
not counted as satellite imagery. All numeric scores are study-specific and should not be ranked across
different tasks.

ELEPHANT MOVEMENT & MIGRATION  |  RESEARCH REVIEW
Search cutoff: 25 October 2026
3
What the papers collectively show
1. Define the ecological target before choosing a model
Seasonal home-range use, dispersal, exceptional long-distance movement, habitat suitability and HEC are
different outcomes. The China case admits competing explanations, while Sri Lankan distribution and fence
studies emphasize local range use and behavioral flexibility. A project should specify which event it predicts
and at what distance and time horizon. [16], [17], [12], [13]
2. Habitat maps are useful, but cannot validate movement
Sri Lankan Landsat and Sentinel studies provide strong environmental and conflict context. Their
classification accuracy or spatial association with incidents does not establish trajectory-prediction accuracy.
Mortality and crop-raiding points are selective observations of a much larger movement process. [2], [3], [4],
[5], [6], [8]
3. Greener or more forested does not always mean better
Udawalawe lost grassland while woody habitats expanded. Malaysian studies show the attraction of
degraded forest and agricultural mosaics. Models therefore need elephant-relevant forage, water, human
risk and barriers, rather than one greenness score standing in for all habitat value. [10], [19], [20]
4. Behavior changes with season, individual and context
Water access, human activity and locomotion costs alter the routes and timing of use. Individual and
ecosystem differences can be substantial, so performance on familiar animals or one landscape may not
transfer. [29], [30], [34], [35], [37], [38]
5. Direct satellite detection remains an observation problem
Very-high-resolution detection is feasible, but independent tests, visibility correction and operational survey
design matter. The 2026 Botswana study exposes the difference between validation performance and
harder test conditions. Counts can change when visibility changes, even without migration. [42], [43], [49]
6. The strongest opening is independent ecological validation
Across the selected work, a defensible contribution is to connect dynamic habitat observations to observed
movement, retain uncertainty and evaluate on unseen animals, places and seasons. Additional network
complexity is useful only if it improves that test and a concrete conservation decision. This is the reviewer's
research-prioritization judgment, not a claim that no earlier study has attempted it. [1], [22], [32], [48], [50]

4
Critical reading of the supplied paper
Keerthanaram and Mahendran (2025), MERCon, pp. 370-374. Reference [1].
Why it is a high-priority starting point
It explicitly connects Sri Lankan satellite image classification, temporal deep learning, deforestation and
elephant migration simulation. Its modular workflow is useful for formulating research questions, and it
reports both land-cover and movement metrics. However, the supplied five-page paper contains specific
inconsistencies that should be resolved before its results are treated as a benchmark.
Movement ground truth is unclear (pp. 371-372)
The introduction and CA subsection claim GPS-trajectory validation, but the data and CA descriptions also
refer to death trajectories and necropsy reports. The collar sample size, tracking duration and separation of
calibration from validation are not clearly stated. Request the actual movement dataset and evaluation split.
Sensor descriptions need correction (pp. 371-372)
The literature review describes Sentinel-2 as a C-band SAR example; Sentinel-2 is optical, while Sentinel-1
carries radar. The methods later name Sentinel-1 correctly. Landsat 8 is also associated with 2000-2023
analysis even though it launched in 2013. Earlier Landsat missions may have been intended, but must be
specified. See technical sources T1-T2.
Spatial resolution and arithmetic need clarification
Red-edge bands are discussed with a nominal 10 m workflow, so native resolution and resampling need
documentation. The reported forest change from 1,850 to 1,615 km2 is a 235 km2 decrease; accompanying
agricultural and urban loss figures need reconciliation with that area accounting.
Some citations do not support the stated evidence
For example, the movement-validation sentence cites the paper's reference [3], a book review of The
Mammals of Sri Lanka, and a lightweight ecological-model discussion points to reference [19], a
sales-forecasting article. These are the source paper's reference numbers, not this review's numbering.
Separate a reported scenario from observed benefit
Projected corridor shifts, regrowth and survival changes should be interpreted as modeled outputs unless
independent field outcomes are documented. The reported classification score does not verify those later
ecological claims.
Recommended use: treat this as a closely matched concept and a list of hypotheses to verify. Reproduction, data clarification and
independent movement validation are prerequisites to relying on its numerical claims.

ELEPHANT MOVEMENT & MIGRATION  |  RESEARCH REVIEW

A practical research direction for Sri
Lanka
Reviewer proposal grounded in the selected literature; feasibility depends on access to movement observations.
Candidate question
Do seasonal satellite-derived changes in forage, surface water and human land use improve short-horizon
elephant movement or crossing predictions over static habitat and proximity models in a Sri Lankan dry-zone
landscape?
Define an outcome that the data can support
With collars, predict held-out next-step use, movement state or crossing probability at a specified horizon.
With systematic camera traps, predict corridor passage over the next day or week. With incident records
alone, study conflict risk and state that limitation; do not relabel the outcome migration. Repeated,
unidentifiable detections support group-use or passage analyses rather than individual paths. [12], [13], [11],
[46], [27]
Combine complementary observations
Extract seasonal land-cover, vegetation and water information from optical imagery; evaluate radar as a
separate cloud-resilient input. Add terrain, tanks, crop calendars, settlements, roads, railways, fences and
gates. Obtain time-stamped movement or standardized passage observations and record missingness and
detection effort. Local field checks should determine whether remotely sensed greenness corresponds to
accessible forage. [2], [3], [7], [10], [29], [35]
Use an interpretable comparison ladder
Begin with persistence, distance-to-water/forest and seasonal baselines. Compare resource or
step-selection models, then circuit or network-based connectivity where appropriate. Add a temporal neural
network only if the sample size and outcome justify it. Compare optical-only, radar-only and fused inputs;
add explicit ablations for water, forage and human activity. [8], [22], [31], [32], [30]
Make the evaluation the main contribution
Hold out complete animals, seasons or geographic blocks as appropriate; avoid splitting overlapping image
patches or neighboring GPS fixes across train and test. Evaluate trajectory or endpoint error for movement,
precision-recall and calibration for passage/conflict, and false alerts per monitoring day for warning systems.
Compare rare excursions and demographic groups separately. Report uncertainty and the effects of missed
observations. [42], [43], [47], [34], [40]
A defensible final output
Deliver a reproducible workflow, an independently evaluated model and seasonal corridor or passage-risk
maps with uncertainty. Validate priority locations with conservation staff and communities and measure
whether the output improves an actual decision. A claim of novelty should follow a final focused literature
check on the chosen landscape, target and validation design. [14], [32], [50]

A / SRI LANKA: HIGHEST GEOGRAPHIC RELEVANCE
[1] Modeling Elephant Migration and Deforestation
Hotspots in Sri Lanka's Dry Forests Using Hybrid
CNN-LSTM Architectures and Cellular Automata
2025 | Thanabalasingam Keerthanaram; Sangeetha Mahendran
Sri Lanka: dry zone | Direct migration-model study
SL | SAT | IP | MOVE
Research and findings (reported)
Combined satellite land-cover mapping with a 3D-CNN-LSTM, cellular automata (CA), and
genetic-algorithm conservation optimization. The paper reports 92.4% land-cover accuracy versus
85.2% for SVM-PCA, movement-model RMSE of 0.8 km and R-squared of 0.76, and a modeled 1.5
km corridor shift under RCP4.5. These are reported results, not independently reproduced. The
classification improvement is 7.2 percentage points.
Gap (reviewer assessment)
The link from classified habitat to independently observed movement is insufficiently documented:
GPS validation is claimed, but the methods also refer to death locations and necropsies, without a
clear collar sample or held-out trajectory design. Mortality points cannot establish individual paths.
Limitations and interpretation
Authors report 48 GPU-hours on an A100 and LiDAR coverage of only 12%. Additional reviewer
concerns include inconsistent sensor descriptions, unclear historical inputs, and limited reproducibility
details. See the dedicated critical-reading page.
Future directions (reviewer synthesis)
Authors propose lighter models, drone LiDAR, additional GPS collars and operational risk maps. First
obtain reproducible inputs and resolve validation inconsistencies; then compare CA with simple
movement baselines on unseen elephants and seasons.
Evidence assessed: Full supplied PDF, pp. 370-374.
10.1109/MERCon67903.2025.11217123 | Full reference [1]

A / SRI LANKA: HIGHEST GEOGRAPHIC RELEVANCE
[2] Identifying human elephant conflict hotspots through
satellite remote sensing and GIS to support conflict
mitigation
2024 | Thakshila D. Gunawansa; Kithsiri Perera; Armando Apan; Nandita K. Hettiarachchi
Sri Lanka: southeast | Conflict hotspot mapping
SL | SAT | IP
Research and findings (reported)
Used Sentinel-2 land-cover classification, MODIS vegetation monitoring and GIS to relate landscape
conditions to reported human-elephant conflict (HEC) in 2021-2022. Random Forest achieved
97.31% overall classification accuracy, compared with 94.62% for SVM. The study locates
conflict-prone interfaces between elephant habitats and human activity rather than reconstructing
individual migration paths.
Gap (reviewer assessment)
High-quality cover maps still need to be connected to actual movement and prospective incident
prediction. A central unanswered question is whether monthly environmental change improves
warning beyond proximity to forests and settlements.
Limitations and interpretation
Incident records depend on reporting and represent harmful encounters rather than all elephant use.
Classifier accuracy does not measure hotspot forecasting accuracy. Two regional landscapes and a
short conflict window constrain transfer to the whole island.
Future directions (reviewer synthesis)
Test future-year hotspot forecasts and transfer to another district, add collar or camera-trap
observations, and report precision-recall and calibration for conflict predictions separately from
land-cover accuracy.
Evidence assessed: Abstract / publisher record.
10.1016/j.rsase.2024.101261 | Full reference [2]

[3] Greenery change and its impact on human-elephant
conflict in Sri Lanka: a model-based assessment using
Sentinel-2 imagery
2023 | Thakshila D. Gunawansa; Kithsiri Perera; Armando Apan; Nandita K. Hettiarachchi; et al.
Sri Lanka | Greenery and conflict assessment
SL | SAT | IP
Research and findings (reported)
Compared SVM, Random Forest and object-based image analysis for Sentinel-2 land-cover mapping,
with official HEC records and vegetation indices. The article discusses 14,897 incidents during
2015-2021 and identifies forest-agriculture interfaces as important conflict settings. In a reported local
analysis, many 2021 incidents fell in open forest or near forest boundaries; the maps provide
environmental context for conflict.
Gap (reviewer assessment)
Greenness is not identical to elephant forage, and an association with incidents does not reveal which
vegetation changes redirect herds. Distinguishing productive crops, scrub, natural grass and
inaccessible vegetation remains essential.
Limitations and interpretation
The imagery and historical incident periods are not fully interchangeable snapshots. Reporting
differences and broad cover classes can affect associations. This analysis does not validate
continuous movement trajectories or demonstrate causal effects of greenery loss.
Future directions (reviewer synthesis)
Use season-matched cover maps, species-relevant forage indicators and water dynamics; evaluate
lagged relationships and independent future incidents. Add movement observations to test whether
greenery predicts route choice or only conflict exposure.
Evidence assessed: Abstract / publisher record.
10.1080/01431161.2023.2244644 | Full reference [3]

[4] Human-elephant conflict and land cover change in Sri
Lanka
2022 | Chithrangani W.M. Rathnayake; Simon Jones; Mariela Soto-Berelov; Luke Wallace
Sri Lanka: nationwide | Land-cover change and conflict
SL | SAT | IP
Research and findings (reported)
Combined official HEC records with Landsat-derived land-cover change for 1993-2018 and
kernel-density hotspot analysis. The authors report that annual incident totals broadly tracked
land-use change and that 98% of recorded HEC occurred within 1 km of recent land-cover change.
Hotspots shifted south and east in the later study years.
Gap (reviewer assessment)
Spatial proximity is strong descriptive evidence but leaves mechanisms unresolved: habitat removal,
crop attraction, infrastructure and reporting access can all produce nearby incidents. The study does
not identify the paths connecting those locations.
Limitations and interpretation
Country-scale historical records can contain location and reporting inconsistencies. A correlation
between nearby change and HEC does not establish causation, and a proximity statistic is not a
forecast evaluated on future data. The underlying observations predate publication by several years.
Future directions (reviewer synthesis)
Update the time series, use matched comparison areas or longitudinal causal designs, and combine
before-and-after satellite change with GPS movement. Benchmark future incident prediction against
simple distance-only models.
Evidence assessed: Abstract / publisher record.
10.1016/j.apgeog.2022.102685 | Full reference [4]

[5] Assessing protected area networks in the
conservation of elephants (Elephas Maximus) in Sri
Lanka
2022 | Chithrangani WM Rathnayake; Simon Jones; Mariela Soto-Berelov; Luke Wallace
Sri Lanka: protected-area network | Protected areas and conflict
SL | SAT | IP
Research and findings (reported)
Evaluated land-use and land-cover change around Sri Lankan protected areas using a
Landsat-derived 1993-2018 change map, together with elephant mortality information. The authors
report that 86% of elephant-death incidents occurred within 5 km of protected areas, highlighting that
conservation performance depends on surrounding human-used landscapes as well as formal
boundaries.
Gap (reviewer assessment)
A mapped boundary does not establish functional connectivity. The unresolved question is which
specific buffer habitats and crossings sustain movement while reducing dangerous interactions
outside protected areas.
Limitations and interpretation
Death locations are a selective outcome and cannot substitute for presence, abundance or route-use
data. Historical land-cover associations do not directly measure the effects of protected-area
designation, fence placement or management quality.
Future directions (reviewer synthesis)
Model protected areas and their buffers as a connected network, validate crossings with telemetry
and cameras, and evaluate land-use interventions around high-risk edges. Separate mortality-risk
prediction from movement-permeability prediction.
Evidence assessed: Abstract / publisher record.
10.1016/j.envc.2022.100625 | Full reference [5]

A / SRI LANKA: HIGHEST GEOGRAPHIC RELEVANCE
[6] The Influence of Habitat Changes on Elephant
Mortality Associated with Human-Elephant Conflict:
Identifying Areas of Concern in the North Central Dry
Zone of Sri Lanka
2021 | Chase A. LaDue; Sarah M. Farinelli; Imira Eranda; Chandana Jayasinghe; et al.
Sri Lanka: northwestern wildlife region | Habitat change and mortality
SL | SAT
Research and findings (reported)
Analyzed necropsies of 348 elephants killed through human activity during 2009-2018 alongside
forest loss, perennial water, precipitation, temperature and population information. Forest loss had
district-specific associations with mortality; water and rainfall also mattered. Emerging hotspot
analysis placed approximately 43% of identified hotspots outside protected areas.
Gap (reviewer assessment)
Mortality reveals where encounters become fatal but not where surviving animals travel. The
district-specific findings leave open how changing water access and forest edges alter movement
before a lethal event occurs.
